surprises: A bare `select{}` used to block a helper child trips Go's own runtime deadlock detector (fatal error, exit 2) because no other goroutine is runnable; the fix is `time.Sleep(24*time.Hour)`, matching the stdlib's own os/exec_test.go `cmdHang` helper.

Go's own os/exec_test.go has moved off the classic GO_WANT_HELPER_PROCESS env-var dispatch this program's GO-TEST-12 rule cites, to an argv[1]-dispatched helper-command registry with unused-helper detection — GO-TEST-12's cited pattern is now the historical shape, not master's current one (both still work; go-testing.md's citation is not wrong, just dated).

The naive 'forward ExitCode() unchecked' bug produces two different wrong numbers depending on where you look: -1 in-process, 255 only after crossing a real os.Exit/OS-wait boundary — a test that asserts -1 without going through an actual subprocess would never catch the 255 a real CLI reports.

top_rules: GO-NET-06's watchdog: time.AfterFunc reset per Read(n>0) + context.WithCancelCause with a typed StallErr cause, on a GO-NET-03 transport clone with ResponseHeaderTimeout set and Client.Timeout=0 — now fixtured and watched.

net/http has no built-in per-Read body idle deadline: IdleConnTimeout bounds pooled-idle connections between requests, ResponseHeaderTimeout bounds only headers — neither bounds a mid-stream stall (go1.27.1 transport.go:229,235).
Reject the SetReadDeadline-conn-wrapper alternative: it requires owning DialContext (conflicts with other dialer customization) and surfaces a generic *net.OpError instead of a typed cause.
Always retrieve the stall with errors.As(context.Cause(ctx), &typed), never ctx.Err()==context.Canceled, which collapses every cancellation reason to one value.

go-containerregistry's remote.WriteLayer/Write never uses the status-code retryTransport for blob PATCH/PUT: uploadOne's tryUpload sets ctx := retry.Never(ctx) before any request (write.go:386), making transport/retry.go's own retry a no-op.

remote.WithRetryStatusCodes is measured INERT on the write path (empty list still retries and succeeds); remote.WithRetryPredicate is the real lever — a never-retry predicate turns the same planted 503 into a hard failure. New GO-NET-17 gap #4.

A retried blob PATCH resends the identical full body via a brand-new upload session (fresh POST+PATCH), not a replay on the same *http.Request; the discarded 503 body is closed via defer resp.Body.Close(), confirmed by only 2 TCP connections across 8 requests.

remote.WithRetryBackoff matters: the unconfigured default (1s/3x/3 steps) costs >=1s wall time on the first retried write (measured 1.006s-1.038s) vs ~15ms with an override — GO-NET-18 stays SHOULD since setup.ocx.sh and the GitHub release CDN returned 200 for every tested User-Agent (Go, Python-urllib default, ocx-sdk-go) on 2026-09-26, contradicting the docstring's 403 claim.
surprises: remote.WithRetryStatusCodes is completely inert for remote.Write/WriteLayer/WriteIndex — it only feeds the low-level retryTransport, which the write path disables via ctx := retry.Never(ctx); only WithRetryPredicate governs write retries.

The write-path retry set is NOT o.retryStatusCodes at all but a separate hardcoded temporaryStatusCodes map in transport/error.go with no public setter — a caller can't add a custom status code to write retries without replacing the whole predicate.

A retried blob PATCH is not a naive resend on a half-consumed reader: go-containerregistry retries the ENTIRE tryUpload closure (fresh POST, fresh upload-session, fresh layer.Compressed() call), so req.GetBody's presence/absence is irrelevant to whether this retry succeeds.

GO-NET-18's premise did not reproduce: neither setup.ocx.sh/dist.json nor the GitHub release asset host returned 403 for any tested User-Agent, including the Python urllib default the fleet's own _dist.py docstring says gets rejected.

The unconfigured go-containerregistry retry backoff silently costs >=1 second of wall time on the very first retried write (measured 1.006s-1.038s) -- easy to eat a CI step's timeout budget without WithRetryBackoff.
No exemplar in the 35-repo corpus implements an idle-read watchdog anywhere; the pattern had zero precedent to measure against, only to build from first principles against go1.27.1 stdlib.

top_rules: GO-REL-03 (never -buildvcs=false) holds unchanged for every fleet shape: submodule, independent nested repo, worktree, and plain clone all stamp correctly when the main package sits at the repo's own top level.
golang/go#74763's real shape is a git repo with no go.mod at its top level plus a nested Go module below it — reproduced verbatim on Go 1.27.1, still open, unfixed, not release-noted.

New SHOULD (GO-REL-15 candidate): before releasing a nested module whose repo has no root go.mod, check `go version -m` for `(devel)` at a tag — -buildvcs=true does NOT turn this into a build error, it stays exit 0.

New SHOULD (GO-REL-16 candidate): never put a main package inside a git submodule or an independent nested git repo's directory — it silently drops ALL vcs.* fields under auto/false and hard-fails under -buildvcs=true.
-buildvcs=auto and -buildvcs=false produce byte-identical `go version -m` output for the submodule/nested-repo-interior failure — banning `false` is orthogonal to that bug, neither cause nor cure.

Git worktrees fully and correctly stamp VCS info on Go 1.27.1 with zero special handling — .git-file/gitdir: support shipped in the Go1.27 milestone (golang/go#58218) — so the fleet's own .agents/worktrees/ dev flow is unaffected.

"multiple VCS detected" and the (devel) degrade are two unrelated Go behaviors; pure git-on-git nesting (submodule, worktree, or plain nested repo) never triggers "multiple VCS detected" under any GODEBUG=allowmultiplevcs setting.

Fixing the monorepo (devel) bug needs a root go.mod AND a nested module path that is a genuine subpath of the root module's path — a root go.mod with a mismatched module name alone still produced (devel).
surprises: The brief's premise conflates two separate Go changes: "multiple VCS detected" (a 1.23.11/1.24.5/1.25rc2 security hardening, GODEBUG=allowmultiplevcs) never fires for any pure-git topology, while golang/go#74763's silent (devel) degrade is a completely different, unrelated code path that has nothing to do with that godebug.

-buildvcs=true does not convert the monorepo-shape (no go.mod at repo root) (devel) bug into a build error — it stays exit 0, silently wrong, which is the opposite of what the flag's name suggests and different from its behavior on the submodule-interior shape (which does hard-fail under =true).

-buildvcs=auto and -buildvcs=false are observably identical (byte-for-byte go version -m output) for the submodule/nested-repo-interior failure mode — GO-REL-11's ban on =false is completely orthogonal to this bug.

An untracked, un-.gitignored independent nested git repo poisons the OUTER build's cleanliness check (+dirty/vcs.modified=true) even though nothing in either repo actually changed — a silent way to accidentally ship a dirty-tagged release for an unrelated reason.

Git worktree support in cmd/go (.git-file/gitdir: pointer recognition) is a Go1.27-milestone feature (golang/go#58218) — newer than most training data would assume — confirmed fully working with zero special handling on the toolchain version this program targets.

A nested-module tag in the correct dir/vX.Y.Z format does NOT fix the monorepo (devel) bug by itself; the root go.mod's module path must also be a genuine parent of the nested module's declared path, which is a stricter requirement than GO-MOD-14's tag convention alone implies.

top_rules: Any cobra command with AddCommand() children MUST also get its own RunE returning a typed usage error, or bare/typo'd invocations silently print help and exit 0 (Runnable()==false hits the same flag.ErrHelp branch as --help, cobra command.go:955-957).

This bug is independent of TraverseChildren/root Args — GO-CLI-17's fix does not reach it; the clause belongs on GO-CLI-06, since cobra's only unknown-subcommand check (legacyArgs) is root-only (args.go:35).

--help and `help <cmd>` are provably unaffected by the fix: execute() checks the help flag before the Runnable() gate, so giving a group a RunE is a risk-free change to the paths that must stay exit 0.

New rule GO-CLI-20: any testable run(args, stdout, stderr io.Writer) entrypoint building a cobra root MUST call root.SetOut(stdout) too, not just SetErr(stderr) — cobra's own help/usage output falls back to the real os.Stdout otherwise, invisible to an in-process test buffer.
The already-shipped go-cli-consolidation/cmd/skeleton/main.go is itself a hit for the SetOut gap (watched via grep, read-only) — the copyable reference example ships the defect.

Contract decided: bare group invocation and a mistyped child print ONE stderr line and exit 64 (like a missing subcommand), never a full usage dump — matching EXIT-03 and GO-CLI-05's one-error-line invariant.

Never rely on Args: cobra.ExactArgs(n)/RangeArgs/MinimumNArgs to catch a mistyped subcommand under a group — it checks token count, not identity (corroborated by openeverest/openeverest#2816, a mechanically distinct sibling bug with the same root cause).

No golangci-lint/staticcheck analyzer understands cobra's Command struct semantics; verification for the core rule is an integration test (given, watched red/green) plus a locator grep for manual confirmation, not a self-contained pass/fail grep.
surprises: The bug is completely independent of TraverseChildren and a custom root Args validator — it reproduces identically on the vanilla, unmodified skeleton shape, contradicting an assumption that GO-CLI-17's root-level fix would also protect nested groups.

A second, compounding, separately-fixable defect exists in the already-published skeleton: it never calls root.SetOut(), so an in-process test harness asserting on the injected stdout buffer sees 0 bytes and exit 0 for ANY cobra-generated help/usage output — the literal 'prints nothing' the brief described, but from a test-harness angle rather than a real terminal (which does receive the text).

--help and `help <cmd>` are structurally guaranteed unaffected by the fix (cobra checks the help flag before the Runnable() gate), so the fix carries essentially zero regression risk on the paths that must stay exit 0 — this was worth actually watching rather than assuming.

A real-world GitHub issue (openeverest/openeverest#2816) independently hit a mechanically distinct sibling bug (Args: ExactArgs(1) + an empty non-nil Run, rather than no Run at all) that converges on the identical root cause and an almost identical fix shape.

cli/cli's own `gh auth` command — the fleet's cited best-practice exemplar throughout go-cli.md for GO-CLI-02/05/06/07/11 — itself carries this exact non-runnable-group defect (pkg/cmd/auth/auth.go has no RunE and 8 AddCommand calls).

There is a genuine, currently-unsettled design fork (not just an oversight) on whether a bare group invocation should be exit-0-with-help or exit-64-with-an-error: both are practiced in real cobra codebases, and neither cobra's own docs nor clig.dev takes a position.

top_rules: Never discard iter.Pull/Pull2's stop func; defer it or route through a reached Close/cleanup — measured a permanent goroutine leak otherwise; no analyzer catches it (GO-LANG-18, MUST).

GO-LANG-08's yield-check MUST does not bind a yield call that is provably the terminal action of its invocation (real, correct idiom in prometheus/promql/parser and bazel-gazelle) — but the exception is fragile and must be reviewed explicitly, never defaulted to.

Route any comparator over a possibly-float type through cmp.Compare/cmp.Ordered, never raw </>: measured slices.SortFunc with a naive comparator producing literally unsorted output once NaN appears (GO-LANG-20, MUST for float-capable types).

Default constraint type elements to ~T unless deliberately restricting to the exact type; the compiler's own error names the fix but only surfaces at a caller's site, not the constraint author's (GO-LANG-19, SHOULD).

comparable-constrained type parameters instantiated with any/interface types can still panic at runtime on an uncomparable dynamic value (e.g. a slice used as a map key via any); the spec states this explicitly and no analyzer catches it (GO-LANG-21, SHOULD).

Deny golang.org/x/exp/constraints via depguard: it is absent from all 35 exemplar repos yet is still the canonical example in Go's own still-live 2022 generics blog post — a stale-source trap for anything trained on it (GO-LANG-22, SHOULD).

Methods cannot declare type parameters below Go 1.27 (exact gate error confirmed); interface methods never can, at any version — the package-level-function-taking-receiver workaround is permanent for interfaces (GO-LANG-23, MUST below floor/for interfaces).

Generic type aliases work fully cross-package at go≥1.23 under the 1.27.1 toolchain; the Go 1.23 release notes' "not yet supported across package boundaries" caveat is stale and corrects a plausible mis-reading of go-language.md's GO-LANG-03.

A generic interface's own type parameter should default to any; push comparable/cmp.Ordered/self-referential constraints onto concrete implementations so the interface doesn't foreclose implementations that don't need them (GO-LANG-24, SHOULD).

The SDK exports []T, never iter.Seq[T], because every collection it produces is already fully materialized before the call returns — iter.Seq earns its place only for genuinely unbounded/lazy/single-use sequences, which the SDK doesn't have (GO-LANG-26, MUST for the SDK).
surprises: The MUST in existing GO-LANG-08 ('every iter.Seq producer must check yield's return value') is overbroad: when the ignored yield call is provably the last action on every path (nothing follows it in that closure invocation), there is genuinely no panic — confirmed with a fixture and found as a real, deliberate idiom in prometheus/promql/parser/ast.go (7 sites in one function) and bazel-gazelle, not a latent bug.

Grepping for explicit `Name[T](...)` instantiation syntax to count generic-function call sites (the natural heuristic, and apparently what the prior go-audit measurement used) undercounts to near-zero for almost every function, because Go's type inference means real calls are written without brackets; switching to `Name(` scoped per-package revealed 15-28 call sites for functions the bracket-only method made look single-use.

Go 1.27 lifted the 'methods cannot have type parameters' restriction — but only for methods on concrete types; interface methods are permanently barred at every version, including 1.27, which the brief's framing (as a flat, version-independent restriction) did not anticipate.

The Go team's own still-live 2022 'Introduction to Generics' blog post uses golang.org/x/exp/constraints.Ordered as its canonical example, five years after cmp.Ordered superseded it — a stale-canonical-source trap baked into a primary, authoritative-looking source.

iter.Pull is essentially unused in the exemplar corpus (6 call sites across 4 of 35 repos, vs 656 iter.Seq occurrences) but is used with perfect stop-discipline everywhere it appears — the risk is real (measured leak) but the corpus shows no actual incidents of it.

A cross-package generic type alias, which the Go 1.23 release notes say is 'not yet supported' across package boundaries, in fact compiles and vets cleanly at a go1.23 module line once built with the go1.27.1 toolchain — the restriction was tied to that release's own compiler, not the module's declared floor, and doesn't reappear later.

Never pool a small value without confirming with -gcflags=-m that it actually escapes -- measured 17x slower with zero allocation benefit when it doesn't escape

surprises: sync.Pool on a small non-escaping struct is 17x SLOWER (+1634%, p=0.000, n=10) with identical zero allocations either side -- the textbook 'pool for speed' pattern is a pure regression when escape analysis already keeps the value off the heap
